cells.tense: Something has finished in you and you can feel it close without needing to know what comes after.
cells.act: let this moment be a fresh entry, not a continuation
cells.ask: This week, let each small ordinary moment — a meal, a walk, a conversation starting — begin fresh rather than arrive as the next piece of the last thing.
cells.core:
You can complete a thing and stay open at the same time. Nothing needs to be held open to be honoured, and nothing needs to be mourned shut. Most people get one half of that; you are standing where both are available.

What feeds this is meeting what arrives while it is still new. Between the ending and the next beginning there is a stretch with no task in it — you do not have to fill it, and you do not have to be sure. Let one ordinary moment this week start fresh instead of carrying the last one in, and then another. A morning before you reach for anything. A conversation in its first minute. You will not have to force the openness; you only have to stop pre-loading the moment with what came before. That is the offer, and it stands whether or not you take it.
cells.sheetLine: You close a cycle and stay open for the next one.
cells.verb: Finishing a cycle fully and letting go into what comes next.
cells.place: Where you release what has served its purpose and clear the space.

cells.tense: You will announce something finished before it has finished, and the announcement will run ahead of the actual ending.
cells.act: receive the thing that is coming instead of bracing for it
cells.ask: When you catch the announcement forming this week, hold still for one slow breath and receive what is actually here, unfinished — then carry on without cancelling anything.
cells.core:
You are closing a cycle before it closes, saying arrived while the road is still under you. It reads from outside as confidence. From inside it is a countdown you cannot pause, and the early finish is how you manage the waiting.

The finishing is real and it is close; what is early is the announcement. The next time you hear it forming — before you say it or write it — hold still and receive what is actually present, partly present. No plan cancelled, no decision made. Then continue. Standing in a door that is still swinging is what tires you. You can receive the coming thing rather than call it done; the door opens on its own schedule, and you do not have to stand in it while it does.

cells.tense: You were standing at a door that has already closed, still asking what comes through it.
cells.act: take the turning as it comes
cells.ask: Write one thing that has already ended in fact — a role, a season, a way of working — on a line by itself, and turn without adding what comes next.
cells.core:
Cycles around you have completed and you are still at the old doorway, looking for the next thing inside it. Something ended — a role, a chapter with someone, a way of working — and it has not been allowed to be finished, because nobody said so, including you. So the next thing arrives late, or does not arrive, while you wait where the door used to be.

Nothing here needs ceremony. Take one that has plainly ended in fact and put it on a line of writing, alone on the page. You will want to qualify it, or write the replacement under it. Leave the page as it is. Letting an end be written is how the turning opens; what releases comes from that, and it is what lets what is next arrive on time rather than overdue.

cells.tense: Your grip releases ahead of you, and you find your hands open without knowing how they got that way.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Set down, deliberately, a weight you have been holding for someone else — a folder, a tab, a worry — placing it the way you would place something on a shelf.
cells.core:
Things end around you and you are already on the next one before anyone says what changed. The release keeps happening; you are just not present for it, and so you cannot tell a letting-go from a loss.

What can be done is small and physical. Take a weight that is not yours — a folder on the desk, a tab you keep open for someone, a worry you have been holding on their behalf — and set it down deliberately. Not by forgetting. On purpose, once, with attention, the way you would place something on a shelf. You will probably go to pick it up again; that moment will be visible to you, and being present for it is the part that is new. When a letting-go is done with your own hands, you get to know it was you who let go.
cells.sheetLine: Your letting-go happens without you there to see it.
cells.verb: Finishing a cycle fully and letting go into what comes next.
cells.place: Where you release what has served its purpose and clear the space.
